summary: `topics` has no `.max()`, but every peer's `decodePresence` truncates the advertised topic list to MAX_RECORD_TOPICS (64). A config with more than 64 topics loads cleanly and then silently under-advertises itself on the presence topic forever.
failure: parseConfig({identity:{handle:'h'}, topics:['ctx-0'...'ctx-69']}) loads (70 topics) and presence-loop.ts:77/92 encodes `topics: allow.topics()` = all 70. Reproduced in-tree: encodePresence(70 topics) -> decodePresence(...) returns topics.length === 64; ctx-64..ctx-69 are dropped by presence.ts:204 `.slice(0, MAX_RECORD_TOPICS)`. Wrong output: every peer's parley_list_users reports this bridge as NOT reachable on its last 6 configured topics, so a hand-off partner never posts there — no error, no log, no warning. The asymmetry is explicit elsewhere: post_topics IS capped at MAX_POST_TOPICS=64 and its docstring says it 'Mirrors the MAX_RECORD_TOPICS cap the presence path already puts on the same shape of untrusted list' — `topics` rides the identical presence field with no such mirror.
remediation: Cap `topics` in the schema at the value the presence record can carry (`.max(MAX_RECORD_TOPICS)`, exported from engine/presence.ts exactly as MAX_POST_TOPICS is used today), so an operator is told at load rather than silently half-advertised. If a longer explicit list must stay legal, make the emitter refuse or warn instead of letting the peer's decoder drop entries.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a config list is emitted onto a wire whose decoder caps it'. Add a table in config.test.ts derived by walking the PresenceRecord fields presence-loop populates (topics, postTopics, and anything added later): for each, build a config at N = wireCap and N = wireCap + 1, encode and decode a beat, and require that either parseConfig rejected N+1 or decodePresence returned every element. Existing coverage is too narrow — config.test.ts's string/numeric walkers only probe scalar leaves and never probe array LENGTH, and allowlist.test.ts's allowlistFor rows use one or two topics.

summary: BackendPlugin.fetchRecent's JSDoc — the frozen, npm-published seam spec — asserts that the SQLite reference backend returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }` for a never-posted topic. It does not.
failure: Trace: packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:238 returns `nextCursor: mintCursor(storeId, servedThrough)` and mintCursor (line 530) is asCursor(`${storeId}.${rowid}`). For a never-posted topic servedThrough is 0n, so the real value is "<storeId>.0", never '0'. An out-of-tree plugin author reading the seam spec and copying the stated shape mints a bare '0' cursor; SQLite's own resumeAfter then treats it as a foreign-store cursor and replays the whole topic. Nothing grades the claim: packages/conformance/src/index.ts:303 deliberately asserts only 'empty page + replayable cursor' without pinning a literal, and no bridge-core test reads this sentence.
remediation: Delete the parenthetical. Replayability is the contract; a specific backend's literal is not, and per CLAUDE.md's prime directive core must not explain itself by pointing at a plugin. If an example is wanted, make it abstract ('e.g. a store-scoped zero position').

summary: The 'no comment or test name in bridge-core names a backend plugin package' case fails with 'core explains itself without naming a backend — dependencies point one way in prose too', but PLUGIN_REFERENCE only matches `bridge-(sqlite|redis|...)`. Core comments name backends freely in every other spelling, so the rule reads as enforced while the class it exists for is wide open.
failure: The guard runs over bridge-core today and passes. Yet seam.ts:120 says 'the SQLite reference backend returns ...', message.ts:60 says 'not always the same value (e.g. Telegram)', engine/catchup.ts:68 says "Discord's 100, Telegram, Matrix /messages", and topic-name.ts:5 enumerates 'NATS subject/stream, Matrix room alias, XMPP MUC JID'. Wrong output: a green case whose failure text claims core names no backend, while the one factually-false instance of exactly that class (the seam.ts finding above) sailed straight through it. The negative-control row ['a backend word that is not a package', 'the postgres backend does this too', false] pins the hole open by design.
remediation: Either widen the matcher to bare product names and fix the offending comments, or narrow the assertion message to what is actually checked ('core names no backend PACKAGE'). A message that overstates its matcher is counted as coverage it does not provide.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'lint message broader than lint regex': for every rule in source-hygiene.test.ts, add a positive-control row feeding the rule's own failure-message claim through its matcher. Concretely, assert PLUGIN_REFERENCE (or a widened successor) fires on every bare name in BACKEND_PACKAGES, with the exemptions enumerated explicitly rather than left implicit in the regex shape.

summary: safeName's digest choice is nowhere pinned inside bridge-core. Mutating createHash('sha1') to 'sha256' leaves the whole bridge-core suite green; only bridge-matrix's fixture, one package away, notices.
failure: Mutation applied at topic-name.ts:59 (sha1 -> sha256). `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/topic-name.test.ts packages/bridge-core/src/stated-bounds.test.ts` -> 105 passed, 0 failed. Only the full repo run reddened, solely in packages/bridge-matrix/test/room-isolation.fake.test.ts ('expected [parley_a_b-c14cddc033] to deeply equal [parley_a_b-3ec69c85a4]'). A shape regex must never be the only assertion on such a value.

summary: SeenSet's LRU recency refresh — the thing that keeps live push-loop topics from being evicted by ad-hoc fetch_recent topics — is covered by a test that never triggers a single eviction, so deleting the refresh entirely leaves the whole bridge-core suite green.
failure: Mutation: in `bucket()` replace the existing-bucket branch (`this.sets.delete(topic); this.queues.delete(topic);` at seen-set.ts:55-56) with an early `return { set, queue }`, turning LRU into insert-order FIFO. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` stays green (2436 passed), and `seen-set.test.ts` alone stays green (13 passed). The guard test 're-touching a topic keeps it alive across a wave of new ones' builds `new SeenSet(4, 8)` and inserts T plus exactly `MAX_TOPICS - 1 = 7` noise topics — 8 buckets total, never exceeding the cap — so the eviction sweep it claims to survive is never reached. The neighbouring 'evicts the coldest topics and keeps the most recent ones' inserts t0..t99 in order, which insert-order FIFO satisfies identically. With the refresh gone, a bridge whose agent reads 256 `post_topics`-matched topics via `parley_fetch_recent` evicts its subscribed push topics and re-emits already-pulled messages as duplicate `<channel>` events — the exact outcome the class docstring promises cannot happen ('the push loop's own topics stay hot').
remediation: Rewrite the hot-topic case so the wave genuinely overflows the cap (e.g. `maxTopics` noise topics, not `maxTopics - 1`), and assert the cold neighbours were the ones dropped. Also assert that `firstSeen`/`has` on a repeat do or do not refresh, whichever the contract intends — today neither is pinned.
testUpgrade: Parameterize an eviction-policy table over (maxTopics, waveSize, touchPattern) with waveSize strictly greater than maxTopics in every row, asserting the survivor SET (not just one member): for each row, build the access sequence, then assert `has()` is true for exactly the k most-recently-*written* topics and false for all others. Drive it from a small generator over waveSize in {maxTopics+1, 2*maxTopics, 10*maxTopics} and interleave patterns {hot-first, hot-last, hot-every-other} so any policy that is merely insertion-ordered fails at least one row. The same shape guards any future bounded cache in core (read-state, roster memoisation).

summary: computeRoster's offline branch must report the FRESHEST instance's topics/postTopics, but the only test of it feeds a single instance, so reducing to the OLDEST beat instead keeps the entire suite green.
failure: Mutation: presence.ts:335 `const from = online ? live : [recs.reduce((a, b) => (b.at >= a.at ? b : a))]` -> `(b.at <= a.at ? b : a)` (pick the oldest instance). Full `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` stays green. The guard test 'an offline handle uses its single last-known beat for topics/reach' posts two beats with the DEFAULT instanceId, so `insts` holds one entry and `recs.length === 1` — the reduce direction is unobservable. Real input that breaks: handle `claude-a` with two offline instances, `inst-old` last beating at now-50s advertising topics ['ctx-old'] and `inst-new` at now-1s advertising ['ctx-new'] (both past ttl, inside sinceMs). Correct output `topics: ['ctx-new']`; the mutant answers `['ctx-old']` while still reporting `lastSeenMs: now-1s`. `parley_list_users` then hands the agent a stale hand-off target with a fresh-looking timestamp, and nothing in the suite notices.
remediation: Add a multi-instance offline row: two or more instanceIds for one handle, differing topics/postTopics, and assert the entry carries the freshest instance's fields while `lastSeenMs` is the max across all of them.
testUpgrade: Table-drive computeRoster over (instances x kinds x ages) rather than over hand-written message lists: rows {1,2,4} instances crossed with {all offline via goodbye, all offline via TTL, mixed online/offline}, each instance given a distinct topic label derived from its age, asserting (a) the reported topics equal the union across LIVE instances when any is online and exactly the freshest instance's when none is, and (b) lastSeenMs equals the max `at` of every retained instance. Every existing single-instance case then becomes the n=1 row, and any future per-instance folding rule (postTopics, a new advertised field) is covered by construction.

summary: The per-process `instanceId` exists solely so a relaunched bridge is not reaped by the old process's trailing `goodbye`, yet no test distinguishes two loops — replacing `randomUUID()` with a fixed literal keeps the whole suite green.
failure: Mutation: presence-loop.ts:80 `const instanceId = opts.instanceId ?? randomUUID()` -> `?? 'fixed'`. Full `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` stays green. The guard test 'stamps a stable per-process instanceId on every beat, defaulting to a fresh random id' asserts only `ids.size === 1` within ONE loop and `!== ''`; a constant satisfies both. Every other presence-loop case injects `instanceId` explicitly, so the default is never compared across loops. With the constant, the exact bug per-instance keying was built to fix returns: process A stops (posts `goodbye` under 'fixed'), process B has already started (posted `hello` under 'fixed'); `computeRoster` keeps the LAST beat per (handle, instanceId), so B's hello is clobbered and a live bridge is reported `online: false` for a whole TTL window (30 min at the documented defaults).
remediation: Assert the property that matters: two `startPresenceLoop` calls with no injected `instanceId` must produce disjoint id sets, and a roster built from loop-A's goodbye plus loop-B's hello must report the handle online.
testUpgrade: Class = 'a defaulted identity/nonce is only tested within one instance'. Add a parameterized cross-instance case that constructs N in {2,3} loops with no injected id, collects every beat, and asserts `new Set(ids).size === N`; then feed those real beats into `computeRoster` and assert online-ness survives the older loop's goodbye. Widen it to any other defaulted per-process token core mints (read-state tmp-file suffix, OAuth nonces) by driving the same table off a list of (factory, extractId) pairs, so a future default that collapses to a constant fails here.

summary: The package README's 'MCP tools exposed' table is stale against transport/tools.ts: it omits `parley_list_users` entirely and `parley_fetch_recent`'s `block_ms`, and its allowlist sentence is false whenever `post_topics` is configured.
failure: `registerTools` (transport/tools.ts) registers FOUR tools; the README table lists three and never mentions `parley_list_users`, which is the whole presence/hand-off surface and is fully documented in the tool description itself. The `parley_fetch_recent` row states the input as `{ topic, since?, limit? }` -> `{ messages, nextCursor }`, omitting the shipped `block_ms` long-poll parameter and the `topicAbsent: true` response field. Worse, README:85 claims 'All three go through the topic `Allowlist` — any topic outside `config.topics` throws `TopicNotAllowedError`.' Trace it: `doPost`/the fetch handler call `allow.assert(topic)`, which returns successfully whenever `Allowlist.has` matches a `post_topics` regex (allowlist.ts:120,124). Concrete input: config `topics: ['ctx']`, `post_topics: ['ops-.*']`; `parley_post({topic: 'ops-eu', ...})` succeeds. An operator reading only this README believes `post_topics` cannot widen the write surface — a security-relevant misreading of the allowlist.
remediation: Regenerate the table from `registerTools`: add the `parley_list_users` row, add `block_ms`/`topicAbsent` to the fetch row, and restate the allowlist sentence as 'the explicit `topics` plus any `post_topics` pattern match, never the reserved presence topic'. Add `post_topics` to the config sample so the widening surface is visible.
testUpgrade: Class = 'a README table drifts from the registered surface'. Add a doc-parity test that registers the tools on an in-memory McpServer, calls `tools/list`, and asserts the set of tool names and each tool's input-schema property names is exactly the set parsed out of the README's tool table — so adding a tool or a parameter fails until the table moves. Pair it with a behavioural row that a `post_topics`-matched topic is ACCEPTED by every tool the README says is allowlist-gated, which pins the sentence rather than the wording.

summary: index.ts publishes `RosterEntry`, `RosterOptions`, `PresenceRecord` and `PresenceKind` but not `computeRoster`, `filterReachable`, `encodePresence` or `decodePresence`, so the types have no reachable producer or consumer — and a sibling package works around it by regex-scraping core's `src/`.
failure: `package.json` publishes only `.` -> `dist/index.js`, and `files: ['dist']`. A consumer can name a `RosterEntry` but cannot obtain one (no `computeRoster`), and can name a `PresenceRecord` but cannot parse a beat into one (no `decodePresence`) or emit one (no `encodePresence`). The concrete downstream consequence is already in the tree: packages/bridge-slack/test/documented-scopes.test.ts:216 states '`computeRoster` is not exported from `@sharptrick/parley-core`, so the mechanism is pinned from its source' and then asserts on the TEXT of `packages/bridge-core/src/engine/presence.ts` with a regex over `emitterOf`'s body. That reaches across a package boundary into another package's unpublished `src/`, and it breaks on a behaviour-preserving refactor (`return rec.handle !== undefined ? asHandle(rec.handle) : m.senderHandle;`) while passing through changes that keep the text shape.
remediation: Either export `computeRoster`/`filterReachable`/`encodePresence`/`decodePresence` (with `MAX_ROSTER_ENTRIES`) alongside the types they operate on, or drop the orphan type exports. Exporting is the smaller change and lets the slack test assert behaviour instead of source text.
testUpgrade: Class = 'a type is on the public surface with no reachable API'. Extend the existing source-hygiene walk (which already derives declared error classes from source and requires each on `index.ts`) with a rule that for every exported `type X` from `engine/`/`transport/`, at least one exported VALUE in `index.ts` mentions `X` in its signature — derived from the source, so a future orphan type fails without anyone naming it. Complement with a lint/test that no test file outside `packages/bridge-core` reads a path under `packages/bridge-core/src/`.

summary: The resume-hint wrapper is deliberately scoped to page 0 (only that page replays a cursor read off disk), but widening it to every page keeps the whole suite green — so the scope is unprotected and a regression would misdiagnose ordinary backend failures as stale-cursor corruption.
failure: Mutation: catchup.ts:54 `page === 0 && resumedFromDisk` -> `resumedFromDisk`. Full `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` stays green. Input that shows the harm: a resumed topic where page 0 succeeds and page 3 fails with a transient `Error('ECONNRESET')`. The operator is then told 'catch-up failed ... while resuming from the stored cursor "c3" ... this backend cannot parse it. Delete <statePath> to re-read from scratch, or give this instance its own instance_id' — advice to delete read-state in response to a network blip, which re-drains and re-emits history. The module comment states the invariant ('Wrap only the first page, so that a later failure ... surfaces as the plain backend error it is') and nothing enforces it.
remediation: Add a case where a resumed catch-up fails on a LATER page and assert the raised message is the plugin's own — no state-path/instance_id advice, and no `cause` wrapper.
testUpgrade: Class = 'a diagnostic is attached at the wrong scope'. Parameterize a table over (resumedFromDisk, failingPageIndex) in {true,false} x {0,1,3}, asserting for each cell whether the surfaced error is the annotated one or the raw plugin error — one predicate, six cells — so any change to which pages carry which diagnostic flips a cell. The same table shape covers the analogous scoping decisions elsewhere (NoSuchTopicError rethrown unwrapped, the MAX_CATCHUP_PAGES warning).

summary: The consent page's redirect-target interpolation is HTML-escaped, but no test pins that escape: deleting escapeHtml at that site leaves all 873 auth tests green while opening a reachable stored XSS on the very page where the owner types the passphrase. REDIRECT_CORPUS exercises this site with eight benign URIs and not one HTML metacharacter; the only hostile-input rows in the suite target client_name.
failure: Mutate `const redirect = escapeHtml(identifyingRedirect(params.redirectUri))` to drop the escape -> `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/auth` = 873 passed (verified). Then, anonymously: POST /register with redirect_uris: ['myapp:">'] -> 201 (the SDK's scheme denylist blocks javascript:/data: but not opaque custom schemes, and WHATWG URL does NOT percent-encode < > " in an opaque path), then GET /authorize?client_id=... renders myapp:"> verbatim (verified: RAW SCRIPT PRESENT: true). Unmutated the same request renders "><script> - so the escape is load-bearing and completely uncovered.
remediation: Add hostile-input rows to REDIRECT_CORPUS (an opaque-scheme URI carrying " < > & ') asserting the raw payload is absent and the escaped form present. Keep the check per interpolation site, not per value: escapeHtml(consentId) is likewise unpinned, harmless today only because consentId is a server-minted UUID.
testUpgrade: Parameterize over (interpolation site x hostile payload): build the table from every value the consent page interpolates - client_name, scopes, redirect target, consent_id, consentPath - crossed with a payload generator ('">

summary: makeOwnerVerifier documents itself as timing-safe (and remote.ts / remote-auth.ts repeat the claim in their public option docs), but replacing timingSafeEqual(actual, expected) with actual.equals(expected) keeps the whole auth suite green. The package already ships the idiom that would catch this - oidc-verifier-wiring.test.ts spies on jose's jwtVerify precisely because 'a policy the verifier expresses as a constant is only a policy if it reaches jose' - but the owner-secret comparator, the single credential that authorizes the bridge, has no equivalent.
failure: Mutate owner.ts `return timingSafeEqual(actual, expected);` -> `return actual.equals(expected);` and run `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/auth` -> 873 passed (verified). No behavioural assertion can see the difference, so the documented timing-safety is enforced by nothing but the reviewer's eye.
remediation: Add a wiring test that mocks node:crypto and asserts makeOwnerVerifier calls timingSafeEqual exactly once per verify, with two 32-byte buffers, on both the match and the mismatch path.
testUpgrade: Generalize to a table of 'declared crypto policy -> primitive it must reach', one row per security-critical delegation in the auth layer: timingSafeEqual in owner.ts, scrypt (async form, with the parsed N/r/p and computed maxmem), jwtVerify options in oidc-verifier.ts, randomBytes(32)/randomUUID in oauth-provider.ts. Each row spies on the module and asserts the exact arguments, so a swap to a non-constant-time, weaker-cost or lower-entropy equivalent fails instead of passing silently.

summary: createOAuthRemoteApp's close() permanently stops the provider's sweep timer and shuts down every rate-limiter MemoryStore, but the transport it wraps documents its own close() as 'idempotent and re-listenable'. A second listen() therefore succeeds and serves the complete OAuth front door with a dead sweeper - no fail-fast, no warning. `pending` is the one store with no lazy eviction (only completeConsent removes an entry), so on a re-listened server every anonymous /authorize leaks a consent record forever.
failure: createOAuthRemoteApp(...) -> listen(p) -> close() -> listen(p): PRM answers 200, provider.sweepTimer._destroyed === true, and a subsequent /register + /authorize leaves provider.pending.size === 1 with nothing that will ever evict it (verified by probe). Expected: the second listen() throws, or close() re-arms the sweeper and the limiter stores.
remediation: Make the contract explicit at the wrapper: latch `stopped` in the composed close() and reject a later listen() with 'this remote auth app has been closed', or re-arm the provider sweeper and allocate fresh limiter stores on listen. Either way, state it in the OAuthRemoteServer doc so it stops contradicting RemoteHttpServer's.
testUpgrade: Extend teardown.test.ts's FACTORIES table (already parameterized over 'close() releases every resource the factory acquired') with a second row-shape: 'the factory's lifecycle contract matches the transport's' - for each factory, close() then listen() and assert either a thrown error or a fully re-armed server (live sweeper, a limiter store whose window still rotates). Driven off the same FACTORIES list, any future front door inherits the check.

summary: Every OAuth response the SDK renders sets Cache-Control: no-store (authorize.js:72, token.js:44, register.js:31, revoke.js:32). Parley's own /parley/consent handler - the response that actually carries the authorization code, in the Location header - sets no cache directive at all, and neither does its 403 error page. RFC 6749 section 5.1 and the OAuth 2.1 BCP treat a response conveying credentials as no-store.
failure: POST /parley/consent with a valid consent_id + passphrase -> 302 with location: http://127.0.0.1:9999/callback?code=c68bb946-...&state=st and no cache-control header at all (verified). Every other endpoint of the same front door returns cache-control: no-store on the same flow.
remediation: Set res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-store') before both the 302 and the 403 branch of the consent handler (or once as middleware on CONSENT_PATH), so the one hand-written endpoint on this AS matches the ones the SDK renders.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'every response of the OAuth front door that carries or gates a credential sets Cache-Control: no-store' table with a row per endpoint (/authorize, /register, /token, /revoke, /parley/consent success, /parley/consent failure) driven through the real flow. That shape also catches the next hand-mounted endpoint; the existing header test only checks the anti-clickjacking trio on the consent page.

summary: assertScopes treats the empty string as a requested scope. The SDK produces it from scope.split(' ') for scope= or for any extra space, so a client sending an empty or loosely-spaced scope parameter is refused with a message that names nothing. RFC 6749's ABNF (scope-token = 1*NQCHAR) means an empty token can never be a scope name, so it should be dropped before the supported-set check rather than reported as an unsupported one.
failure: GET /authorize?...&scope= (or scope=mcp  mcp) -> 302 to the client with error=invalid_scope&error_description=this server does not issue the scope(s) ; it supports mcp (verified against a live app). The named scope is the empty string, so the message tells the client nothing about what it did wrong and the flow is unrecoverable without reading this source.
remediation: Filter empty tokens before the check ((scopes ?? []).filter(Boolean)), keeping the strict refusal for every genuinely-named unsupported scope. Same treatment on the refresh-narrowing subset check, which rejects scope= identically.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the scope table over a whitespace/degenerate generator instead of the two happy values: '', ' ', 'mcp ', ' mcp', 'mcp  mcp', 'mcp\tmcp', 'MCP', 'mcp admin' - asserting for each row both the outcome (accepted with a normalized scope set, or invalid_scope) and that any error_description names at least one non-empty token. Run the same rows through /authorize and through the refresh-token scope parameter, since both split the same field.

summary: The poll tick checks `this.stopped` only once, before the SELECT. If the consumer's handler tears the plugin down, the loop keeps invoking the handler for every remaining row of the batch after `disconnect()` has closed the driver, cleared the statements and marked every subscription `stopped`.
failure: connect(poll_interval_ms:10); subscribe(T, handler) where the handler calls `p.disconnect()` on its first message; post 'a','b','c','d'. Measured: handler receives ['a','b','c','d'], of which ['b','c','d'] arrive AFTER disconnect() resolved — while `subscriptionHealth()` already reports state 'stopped'/lastError 'disconnected' and `post()` rejects with 'not connected'. Core's contract (conformance ASSERTED_PROPERTIES 'disconnect-stops-live-delivery') and the README's 'After disconnect() every topic reads stopped' both say nothing may reach a handler afterwards; an embedder that shuts down on an inbound control message keeps emitting <channel> events for a backend it believes is gone.
remediation: Re-check the cancellation flag inside the per-row loop, not just at the top of the tick: `for (const row of rows) { if (this.stopped || this.driver === undefined) return; lastSeen = row.id; ... }`. Same guard belongs anywhere a synchronous fan-out can re-enter the plugin.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized conformance clause 'nothing reaches a handler after disconnect(), including from a handler-initiated teardown', driven over a table of teardown triggers x batch positions: {trigger: 'handler calls disconnect', 'external disconnect during settle', 'disconnect twice'} x {rows pending: 1, 2, POLL_BATCH} — asserting the handler count is frozen at the index where teardown began. The existing conformance case only disconnects from OUTSIDE the handler with no batch in flight, so no row can be pending when the flag flips and it cannot fail.

summary: `recordCatchUp` inserts into `caughtUpThrough` on every `fetchRecent`, keyed by the caller-supplied topic, with no bound and no eviction until `disconnect()`. With a `post_topics` regex (which core admits for fetch_recent), the set of reachable topics is unbounded, so a long-lived remote/chat bridge accumulates one entry per distinct topic ever fetched. Core deliberately refuses this exact shape one layer up (transport/push-loop.ts: "a per-topic ledger would be an unbounded map keyed by untrusted input").
failure: config with `post_topics: ["ctx-.*"]`; call parley_fetch_recent for topic `ctx-0` … `ctx-N`. Measured directly against the plugin: 500 distinct fetch topics -> `caughtUpThrough.size === 500`, none of which is ever removed. The values are only meaningful for topics that are or will be subscribed (the explicit `topics` list); every other entry is pure growth in a process DESIGN §10 expects to be long-lived.
remediation: Only record a hand-off point for topics that can be subscribed — the explicit allowlist — or cap the map (e.g. drop the entry once a subscribe for that topic has been armed, or bound it with LRU eviction and fall back to `maxId(topic)` on a miss, which is already the correct answer for a topic catch-up never read).
testUpgrade: Add a class-level test 'no plugin state grows with the number of distinct caller-supplied topics': loop N=2000 fetchRecent calls over fresh topic names and assert every internal Map/Set/Array on the plugin stays bounded (walk own properties, assert `size`/`length` <= a constant). Parameterize over the caller-facing entry points that take a topic (fetchRecent, post, subscribe) so a future ledger added on any of them is graded by the same case.

summary: The only thing grading `precreate()` — the README's security claim that the store 'is claimed at 0600 *before* the driver opens it, so it is never briefly world-readable' — is the `absent` row's expectation that no 'tightened' line was printed. That is an artefact of the runner's umask, and CI pins no umask.
failure: Delete `if (onDisk) precreate(path);` from src/driver.ts (i.e. remove the entire pre-creation window guarantee) and run `umask 077; npx vitest run packages/bridge-sqlite/test/at-rest-mode.test.ts` -> 12/12 PASS. Under the container's default umask 022 the same mutation goes red, so whether the claim is graded at all depends on the environment the suite happens to run in. Neither .github/workflows/ci.yml nor vitest.config.ts sets a umask.
remediation: Make the test own the umask instead of inheriting it: set `process.umask(...)` per case (restoring it after) and parameterize the whole PRE_EXISTING table over [0o022, 0o077, 0o000]. Better still, grade the window directly — assert the mode of a freshly created store immediately after `precreate` and before `openConnection`, rather than inferring it from the absence of a diagnostic line.

summary: `describe('every accepted retention_days actually prunes')` asserts only that no `retention prune failed` line reached stderr. Five of its six rows plant a row that is INSIDE the window they configure, so nothing is ever pruned in them; the block cannot distinguish 'prunes correctly' from 'does not prune at all'.

summary: `retention_days` rejects `0` and negatives by name because they 'would delete the entire history', but accepts any positive value however small — and `connect()` prunes immediately. A value numerically indistinguishable from 0 produces exactly the irreversible outcome the guard exists to prevent, with the same fail-fast message conspicuously absent.
failure: Post 'important' to a store, then `connect({ db_path, retention_days: Number.MIN_VALUE })`. Measured: connect() succeeds and the immediate prune leaves 0 messages — the whole shared file, every session's history, gone, no diagnostic. `retention_days: 0` under the same conditions is refused with a message about irreversible deletion. `1e-9`, `1e-12` and YAML's `1e-3` behave the same way. Given how carefully everything else here refuses to take an irreversible action on a mistyped value (unknown keys, non-integer poll intervals, unrepresentable cutoffs), a self-hoster reasonably reads 'a bad retention value is refused' as covering this.
remediation: Make the guard match the hazard rather than the sentinel: reject a window whose cutoff is not strictly in the past by a meaningful margin (e.g. require `retentionDays * 86_400_000 >= 1000`, or refuse any window shorter than the poll interval), naming the same 'omit the key to keep every message forever' escape. testUpgrade: Turn the accept/reject decision into one boundary table read from the exported constant that defines the floor, with rows straddling it: [0, -1, MIN_VALUE, 1e-12, floor/2, floor, floor*1.5, 0.5, 30, 1e6] x {rejected-by-name, accepted-and-store-survives-a-pre-existing-message}. The class is 'a validator that rejects a sentinel while accepting values with the identical effect'; the same table shape should be applied to poll_interval_ms and to any future bounded knob.

summary: The frozen conformance suite — the project's certification that this backend satisfies the seam — is run once, against whichever driver `openDriver` resolves, which in CI is always better-sqlite3. The `node:sqlite` fallback is exactly what a user whose platform has no prebuilt binary runs (better-sqlite3 is an optionalDependency), and it is graded only by driver-parity.test.ts's five narrow cases (pragma read-back, at-rest mode, RunResult shape, one seam round-trip).
failure: No live defect: I hid node_modules/better-sqlite3 and re-ran the suite — the fallback passes all 32 clauses today (restored afterwards). But the coverage claim is wrong: paging at every limit, exclusive-since, cursor/backendMsgId agreement across live and catch-up, the 0-3 ms blocking-fetch race, the interleaved-writer case and the multi-process case are certified for one driver only. A future divergence in bigint parameter binding (`resumeAfter` binds a BigInt), in `changes`/`lastInsertRowid` typing (prune's `Number(info.changes) >= PRUNE_BATCH`), or in `all()` row prototypes would ship green, and the README's 'the plugin code above the driver doesn't care which one is active' would be a promise nothing grades.
remediation: Parameterize the conformance factory over the driver: run `runConformanceSuite('sqlite (better-sqlite3)', …)` and `runConformanceSuite('sqlite (node:sqlite)', …)`, using driver-parity.test.ts's existing `loadWithout(['better-sqlite3'])` module-reset trick to force the fallback, and keep the hard assertion that both drivers are loadable so a missing one reds rather than skips.

The class is 'a shipped runtime variant the ratchet never exercises' — the same widening applies to any other environment-selected implementation (e.g. if a second JSON/YAML loader or a second transport is ever selected by availability rather than by config).

summary: An entry whose stream-id millisecond component is a safe integer but past the ECMAScript Date range (>8.64e15) makes `entryTimestamp` call `new Date(ms).toISOString()`, which throws RangeError — permanently wedging catch-up for that topic and silently dropping the entry on the live path.
failure: Reproduced against a live Redis: `XADD parley:wedge 9000000000000000-0 sender mallory content hi` (any explicit id in 8640000000000001..9007199254740991, i.e. a safe integer the `Number.isSafeInteger` guard lets through), then `plugin.fetchRecent({topic: 'wedge'})` rejects with `parley-redis: Invalid time value (topic wedge, key 'parley:wedge')`. The entry is durable, so EVERY later fetchRecent on that topic throws forever — core's catchUpTopic rethrows it and aborts catch-up for the topic. On the subscribe path the same throw is swallowed by the handler's best-effort catch, so the message is dropped with no diagnostic at all. README's own threat model says anyone with Redis access can XADD, and `rowToMessage`'s doc comment promises exactly the opposite of this behaviour.
remediation: Clamp the id-derived millisecond to the representable Date range before constructing (e.g. `ms >= 0 && ms <= 8_640_000_000_000_000 ? ms : 0`), and make `rowToMessage` total: no field or id a foreign writer can choose may throw out of fetchRecent/subscribe. Consider funnelling both paths through one `safeIso()` helper so the live and catch-up halves cannot diverge.
testUpgrade: The foreign-writer table in test/live-failure-modes.test.ts fixes the id at `'*'` on every row, so the entire id axis is ungraded — deleting the isSafeInteger guard leaves all 594 tests green. Cross the existing field rows with an ENTRY-ID axis written explicitly: `1-0`, `${Date.now()}-0`, `8640000000000000-0` (last representable), `8640000000000001-0` (first out of range), `9007199254740993-0` (first unsafe integer), `${2n**64n-1n}-${2n**64n-1n}`, and assert for each, on BOTH fetchRecent and subscribe, that the message arrives and `timestamp === new Date(Date.parse(timestamp)).toISOString()`. The class is 'a value a foreign writer chooses is used as arithmetic input' — generate ids from the uint64 bound rather than hand-picking them.

summary: When `connect()` fails on the whole-handshake deadline, `client.disconnect()` is called while the handshake is still in flight and the TCP socket is never destroyed — it stays ESTABLISHED and remains an active handle, and nothing retains the client so no later `disconnect()` can reclaim it. This is the exact hazard the reader path documents and guards with the `connecting` set.
failure: Reproduced: a `net.createServer` that accepts and never speaks RESP; `plugin.connect({url, connect_timeout_ms: 300})` rejects with `parley-redis: cannot reach …` three times → the server still holds 3 ESTABLISHED sockets 1.5s later, and `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` shows +1 `TCPSocketWrap` per attempt that survives a subsequent `plugin.disconnect()`. Control: the same stall applied to a READER (blocking fetchRecent through a stalling proxy) returns its socket immediately, so the leak is specific to the command client's failure path. Real-world trigger: a load balancer in front of a dead Redis, a TLS-only listener addressed as `redis://`, or any `connect_timeout_ms` shorter than a loaded server's handshake — one leaked fd and one event-loop handle per attempt.
remediation: Give the command client the same protection the readers have: track it in `connecting` (or await the settlement of the `client.connect()` promise) and destroy the socket only once the handshake has settled — e.g. `withDeadline(...).catch(async e => { await connectPromise.catch(()=>{}); await client.disconnect().catch(()=>{}); throw e; })`, or keep a reference and close it on the next `disconnect()`. Whatever the shape, a failed `connect()` must leave zero sockets.
testUpgrade: The 'lifecycle must not leak connections' class in test/live-failure-modes.test.ts counts sockets on the proxy but every row starts from a SUCCESSFUL connect, and the 'tcp accepts but never speaks redis' row in failure-modes.test.ts asserts only the rejection. Parameterize the socket-count assertion over lifecycle calls that FAIL: {connect(), connect()·subscribe(), connect()·blocking fetchRecent()} × {deadline fires during TCP connect, during the RESP handshake, during the verifying PING} × {1, 3 attempts}, asserting `proxy.live() === 0` and no growth in `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` after each. The class is 'a failure path that opens a socket must return it', not this one endpoint.

The `core-catchup.test.ts` `rig()` helper is the shape the rest of the files want and do not use.

summary: A single failed drain query permanently drops that batch from the live path. `drain()` swallows the error, leaves `lastSeen` unadvanced, and the only re-entry points are a *future* NOTIFY on the same channel or a listener-connection reconnect — neither of which is guaranteed to happen. Postgres is the only backend whose subscribe is purely edge-triggered: bridge-sqlite explicitly escalates to a degraded poll after consecutive failures (src/index.ts:81-83), bridge-redis re-loops. This one has no retry at all.
failure: Subscriber live on quiet topic T with lastSeen=5. A post commits seq=6; the AFTER INSERT trigger's NOTIFY arrives while a pooled read is transiently failing (role/database `statement_timeout`, a `pg_terminate_backend` of one pooled backend, a pgbouncer server-side disconnect, deadlock). The listener socket is untouched, so no 'end' fires and no reconnect re-drain happens. `drain()` catches, sets `draining=false`, and returns. seq=6 is durably stored and never reaches the handler — no `<channel>` event, no error anywhere — until some unrelated later post to T rings the doorbell again. Reproduced: with the shared `fake-pg` Pool made to reject once during the drain and restored immediately, the handler received `[]` where `['lost']` was expected, and stayed empty for 500ms after recovery. This also contradicts the class JSDoc at src/index.ts:276-279 ('a coalesced, dropped or mis-addressed notification costs latency and never a message') and the inline comment at 945-946 that asserts the recovery as fact.
remediation: Make drain failure recoverable rather than terminal: on a caught error, re-arm a bounded backoff retry for that subscription (unref'd timer, cleared by `disconnect()` and epoch-guarded like every other chore), or add a low-frequency per-topic safety re-drain so the live path converges the way sqlite's degraded poll does. Delete the comment at 945-946 or make it true.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a transient backend failure on the push path is silently terminal' with a parameterized case over (failure site x failure count x whether a doorbell ever rings again): failure sites = {drain read, reconnect re-drain read, waiter re-check}; counts = {1, 3, until-recovered}; doorbell = {never rings again, rings once after recovery}. Every cell asserts the row is delivered to the live handler within a bounded budget with NO further NOTIFY emitted. The existing background-tasks.test.ts row 'drain after a failing pool' is too narrow — it asserts only that `fetchRecent` still works afterwards, i.e. it grades the read path, not the push path the drain belongs to, so this defect survives it green.

summary: `startSubscription`'s tail read (`SELECT COALESCE(MAX(seq),0) …`) is the one statement in `subscribe()` not wrapped by `listenerUnavailable`, so a pooled-connection failure there rejects `subscribe` with the bare driver string. `listenerUnavailable`'s own JSDoc (src/index.ts:198-204) states exactly why that must not happen: core's push loop rethrows anything that is not a `NoSuchTopicError`, so the whole bridge fails to come up on a message naming neither the backend nor the topic.
failure: With the pool made to reject the `MAX(seq)` read with a realistic driver message, `plugin.subscribe(asTopic('quiet'), …)` rejects with `terminating connection due to administrator command` — no `parley-postgres:` prefix, no topic name. listener-blackout.test.ts asserts `/^parley-postgres:/` and `toContain(String(target))` for the reject arm, but only ever fails the LISTEN connection, never the pooled tail read, so this path is ungraded.
remediation: Wrap the tail read in the same `try { … } catch (err) { throw listenerUnavailable(topic, err); }` as the two calls surrounding it (or introduce one wrapper around the whole of `startSubscription`'s body), so every way `subscribe` can fail names the plugin and the topic.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a seam call fails with a raw driver string' by parameterizing listener-blackout.test.ts over the failing SURFACE as well as the window: surface = {listener connect, LISTEN query, pooled tail read, pooled drain read}. Every cell whose declared arm is 'rejects' asserts `/^parley-postgres:/` and that the message contains the topic. Derive the surface list from the awaits in `startSubscription` so a new statement added there is a missing row rather than silence, exactly as lifecycle.test.ts pins `EPOCH_GUARD_SITES`.

summary: The full 32-case conformance suite is run twice — once with a short `table_name`, once at `MAX_TABLE_NAME_BYTES` — but the name length can only affect one thing on a real server: whether the derived relation names survive PostgreSQL's 63-byte identifier limit during bootstrap. Once `connect()` returns, cursor arithmetic, paging, dedup, blocking fetch, concurrency and push behave identically. So 32 of the 64 cases cost ~5.5s and cannot independently fail.
failure: Every clause other than bootstrap is a near-copy: e.g. 'seam conformance: postgres (52-byte table_name) > catch-up since a cursor returns only newer messages (exclusive)' cannot fail for any reason the short-name row would not also fail for. Conversely the property the long row exists for is already pinned twice at unit level — schema.test.ts iterates every accepted length asserting each derived relation is ≤63 bytes and mutually distinct, and `assertTableName` rejects `'a'.repeat(MAX_TABLE_NAME_BYTES + 1)` and `'a'.repeat(62)`.
remediation: Run the conformance suite once. Move the real-server long-name coverage into table-name.test.ts, which already drives connect → subscribe → post → fetchRecent → resolveIdentity → NOTIFY end to end per name: add `'a'.repeat(MAX_TABLE_NAME_BYTES)` as one more row in its `NAMES` corpus. That keeps the only thing the second run bought (a real server accepting the maximal DDL, including the auto-generated `<table>_senders_pkey` that overflows 63 bytes and is truncated) at one case instead of thirty-two.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a config dimension is exercised by re-running a whole suite instead of by the one path it reaches' with a single parameterized real-server smoke case per accepted `table_name` shape (reserved words, MixedCase, 1 byte, MAX_TABLE_NAME_BYTES) that drives every seam method once — and reserve `runConformanceSuite` for one representative context. Widen table-name.test.ts's `NAMES` generator from the exported `MAX_TABLE_NAME_BYTES` so a narrowed budget automatically re-tests the new maximum.

summary: The README hard-codes five numbers that the source derives or exports, with nothing binding them: `52 bytes` (MAX_TABLE_NAME_BYTES, computed from DERIVED_SUFFIXES), `18250` (MAX_RETENTION_DAYS), `batches of 5000 rows` (PRUNE_BATCH), `lock_timeout = 5000` / `gave up after 5000ms` (LOCK_WAIT_MS), and `pool_size 5`. All are correct today; all silently rot on the next tune. This package derives everything else on principle — suite-hygiene.test.ts reads the shared-helper list out of the harness precisely because 'a hand-kept list drifts' — and the README is the one surviving hand-kept copy, on the surface that ships to npm.

The same holds for lowering PRUNE_BATCH or LOCK_WAIT_MS — the README keeps promising the old number with no test anywhere going red.

Either template the numbers out of `MAX_TABLE_NAME_BYTES` / `MAX_RETENTION_DAYS` / `PRUNE_BATCH` / `LOCK_WAIT_MS` at doc-build time, or add a docs test asserting each documented figure equals its exported constant — the constants are already exported, which is otherwise their only consumer besides tests.

Extend the same rule to every other doc-visible constant the package exports.

summary: `recentWindow` mints `@parley-stream:` (empty token = "first visible event in the room") whenever it reads zero pages, which regresses a caller's cursor to the beginning of the room instead of leaving it where it was.
failure: Reproduced with the shipped fake: connect, `post(t,'a')`, `post(t,'b')`, then `const pending = p.fetchRecent({topic:t, limit:10}); await p.disconnect(); await pending` → `{messages: [], nextCursor: "@parley-stream:"}` (a healthy call on the same topic returns `$e1:fake`). `catchUpTopic` (packages/bridge-core/src/engine/catchup.ts) calls `readState.set(topic, nextCursor)` unconditionally, so a SIGINT landing in startup catch-up persists "beginning of room" to read-state; the next start drains the whole room from event 0 with a fresh SeenSet and re-delivers every message into agent context. In `shared_room` mode that is every topic's history. The same path is reached via the expired-cursor fallback (`fetchSince` 404 → `recentWindow`), which replaces a valid stored cursor.
remediation: `recentWindow` must only mint a position it actually read. Thread the caller's `since` (or `undefined`) in, and when the paging loop executed zero iterations — `isStale(generation)`, `limit <= 0`, or a response with no `start` token — return that incoming cursor rather than `asCursor(STREAM_CURSOR_PREFIX)`. The `roomId === undefined` early return in `fetchRecent` is the only place an empty stream token is legitimate, because there is provably no history behind it.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every seam call that returns EMPTY must return a cursor that is at-or-after the caller's position, never before it. Add a parameterized case over the cross-product of {no `since`, `since` = a minted event id, `since` = a minted stream token, `since` = a purged id} x {short-circuit = disconnect at the `existingRoom` await boundary, disconnect mid-page, `/messages` 500, stale generation via a bare `connect()`}: seed the room with history, drive the read, and assert that `nextCursor` is either the incoming cursor or one that replays to strictly fewer messages than the room's full history — i.e. `fetchRecent({since: nextCursor})` never returns a message the caller already had. `recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts`'s 'mints a cursor that stays put' rows are too narrow: they only exercise the healthy path, where the loop always runs at least one page.

summary: In `subscribe`'s loop only the fetch/parse is inside the try; the first dereference of the parsed body (`json.next_batch`) is outside it, so a `/sync` body of JSON `null` throws out of `void loop()` as an unhandled rejection — killing the process under Node's default and, at best, silently ending the live path with no retry and no stderr report.
failure: Reproduced: stub `fetch` so incremental `/sync` (any request carrying `since`) answers `200` with body `null` and `content-type: application/json`. After `await p.subscribe(t, handler)` the process emits `unhandledRejection: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'next_batch')`. `res.json()` succeeds (it is valid JSON) so the retry/backoff ladder at lines 896-901 never sees it; the loop just disappears. Node 22 defaults to `--unhandled-rejections=throw`, so an MCP stdio bridge terminates.
remediation: Move every use of the parsed body inside the `try` (or validate the shape at the parse site: reject anything that is not a non-null object and route it through `reportSyncFailure` + `syncRetryDelayMs` like any other `/sync` fault). Additionally attach a `.catch()` to `void loop()` so no future throw inside the loop can become an unhandled rejection rather than a reported, backed-off failure.
testUpgrade: CLASS: no malformed-but-parseable upstream response may escape a fire-and-forget background loop. Add a table over `/sync` response bodies {`null`, `[]`, `"string"`, `123`, `{"rooms":null}`, `{"rooms":{"join":"x"}}`, `{"next_batch":42}`} x {subscribe loop, dedicated bounded `/sync` behind a blocking fetchRecent}, each asserting (a) zero `unhandledRejection` events on `process`, and (b) the loop keeps polling and still delivers a subsequent well-formed message. `subscribe-resilience.fake.test.ts` only injects HTTP statuses and network rejects — both land inside the try — so it cannot reach this class.

summary: The `M_ROOM_IN_USE` create/resolve race recovery in `resolveOrCreateRoom` has zero coverage: the fake's `POST /createRoom` returns 200 with the existing room for an alias already taken (real Synapse returns 409), and the live conformance fixture deliberately pre-warms the room so the race never happens.
failure: Mutation: delete the whole `const raced = await this.lookupAlias(alias); if (raced !== undefined) { await this.joinRoom(raced, alias); return raced; }` block from `packages/bridge-matrix/src/index.ts:1163-1167`, so a lost create race throws `createRoom failed (409) and alias unresolved` instead of resolving and joining. The live suite cannot catch it either — `conformance.test.ts`'s `concurrentPost` comments say it pre-warms "so the W writers only resolve+join, never race W creates", and `live-per-topic.test.ts` is sequential. So CLAUDE.md's "multi-process writes don't corrupt or error" criterion is unverified for Matrix: two bridge instances first-posting to the same topic simultaneously exercise a branch nothing grades.

Fix any behaviour that exposes, then keep the fake honest.

Parameterize over {shared_room, per-topic} x {createRoom 409 then alias resolves, createRoom 409 then alias still 404, createRoom 400 then alias resolves} x {entry = post, entry = subscribe}: assert exactly one room exists, that the loser JOINed it and returns the same `room_id` the winner did, that a 403 on that join still names the alias/MXID/fix, and that the unresolvable case throws carrying the homeserver body. Also add a concurrency row driving N plugins' first `post` to one fresh topic through `Promise.all` and asserting `fake.rooms` has length 1 and every message landed in it.

summary: The README claims "a `fetch_recent` with no `since` is the default recent window and returns at once, even on a topic whose room does not exist yet" — core's `fetch_recent` tool does the opposite and holds for the full `block_ms`.
failure: An agent calls the `fetch_recent` tool with `block_ms: 60000` and no `since` on a topic whose room does not exist. Per the README it returns immediately. In fact `packages/bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:230` routes any `block_ms > 0` through `fetchRecentBlocking`, whose contract (packages/bridge-core/src/engine/blocking-fetch.ts) is explicitly "Blocking engages whenever the queried window comes back EMPTY, with or without a `since` … on an empty topic it waits out the budget like any other", and the tool description core ships to the model says "if the queried window is empty — whether or not you passed `since` — the call holds". Core's second iteration passes `since = nextCursor`, at which point MatrixPlugin's own native park engages via `roomForRead`. The tool call therefore blocks 60s. bridge-matrix is the only package README carrying this extra sentence; the other eight stop at the shared `catchup.block_max_ms` paragraph.

testUpgrade: CLASS: a per-backend README describing core-owned tool semantics. summary: Every read path joins the topic's room via `existingRoom` → `joinRoom`, nothing in `src/` ever leaves or forgets a room, and the resulting joined-room growth degrades every `/sync` — a cost the repo measures in a test helper but the README never mentions.

The project's own `packages/bridge-matrix/test/live-gate.ts:retireRoom` records the consequence: "`existingRoom()` joins and nothing ever leaves, and every `/sync` degrades with the size of that set (a session was measured going from 3.4s to over 15s), which reads as a flaky homeserver rather than as accumulated fixtures." A long-lived deployment therefore slows monotonically and the operator has no documented lever.
remediation: Document it in the README next to "Reads never provision" — a read does not create a room but it does JOIN one, joins are permanent, and the joined-room set is what bounds `/sync` latency — and say what the operator does about it (leave rooms for retired topics out-of-band, or scope `topics`/`post_topics` patterns tightly). Pair it with a doc-parity assertion that the README's "Reads never provision" paragraph names `join` as the side effect a read DOES have.

summary: A since-less fetchRecent whose window contains no bodied item reports the ZERO cursor '' — a cursor that means "from the very beginning of the archive" — instead of the window's real tail, so the next call replays the whole room history.
failure: Reproduced with the package's own fixture. Archive = [m1(body 'old-1'), m2(body 'old-2'), s1(subject, no body), s2(subject, no body)]. `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 2})` first returns `{messages:['old-1','old-2'], nextCursor:'arch-2'}`. After the two bodiless items land, the identical call returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: ''}` — the cursor went BACKWARDS past two messages it had already issued. `readWindow` (line 603) takes the last `limit` archive rows and `.filter(hasBody)`s them to nothing, and line 588 then falls through to `args.since ?? asCursor('')`. Core stores that in read-state (engine/catchup.ts:66 `readState.set(topic, nextCursor)`), and the next start calls `fetchRecent({since: ''})`, which `mamQuery` deliberately turns into a query with NO `<after/>` — a full re-read of the archive from message one. Reachable on a real server via MAM tombstones (XEP-0424 retraction) or any archived stanza with no <body>; the plugin, its README ("admission") and archive-admission.test.ts all model bodiless archive rows as a first-class case.
remediation: Make the cursor the window's UNFILTERED tail on BOTH arms, exactly as `exclusiveMam` already does for its paging `<after>`: have `readWindow` return the raw page tail alongside the bodied items and use `rawTail?.archId ?? args.since ?? ''` at line 588. An empty archive still yields '' correctly; a window of nothing-but-unadmitted items then advances instead of rewinding.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a page whose admitted set is empty must never move the cursor backwards" by parameterizing archive-admission.test.ts's existing 'advances the catch-up cursor past a page of stanzas it does not carry' case over the `since` arm — {undefined, zero cursor '', a real archive id} — crossed with tail composition {all bodied, mixed, all bodiless, whole archive bodiless}. Each row asserts the returned nextCursor is either the caller's own cursor or a cursor no earlier than one the plugin previously issued for that topic (drain-then-replay: feeding it back must not return a message already returned). Today that case only ever drives the `since`-given arm, which is why the `since`-less arm regressed unseen; the conformance clause 'a since-less fetch returns the NEWEST messages' also never puts an unadmitted stanza at the tail.

summary: `isPlaintextRemote` returns false for any `service` without a URI scheme, so the cleartext-SASL-PLAIN warning is silent for the standard schemeless (DNS-SRV) service form — which @xmpp/resolve happily falls back to plaintext xmpp:// on port 5222.
failure: `backend_config: { service: "chat.example.com", password: "real-secret" }`. Verified: `isPlaintextRemote('chat.example.com') === false`, `isPlaintextRemote('example.com') === false`, `isPlaintextRemote('xmpp.example.com:5222') === false` (the scheme regex matches `xmpp.example.com:` as a "scheme", which is simply not in PLAINTEXT_SCHEMES). connect() therefore prints no SECURITY line. But node_modules/@xmpp/resolve/index.js:60 routes any service with no `://` through SRV discovery, and lib/dns.js:28 puts `xmpp://<ip>:5222` in the candidate list — `fallbackConnect` walks to it whenever xmpps/5223 is closed, and @xmpp/client registers SASL PLAIN unconditionally. Result: the password crosses the network in the clear with the exact diagnostic this function exists to emit suppressed. The creds-warning table (166 rows) covers only scheme-prefixed services, so the whole host-form axis is untested.
remediation: Treat an absent scheme as UNKNOWN transport, not as safe: if the trimmed service contains no `://`, extract the bare domain and apply the same loopback test, warning for anything non-loopback (SRV can and does resolve to plaintext). Better still, also warn from the client's `status`/`connecting` event on the URI actually negotiated, so the warning reflects the socket rather than the config string.
testUpgrade: Add a HOST-FORM axis to creds-warning.test.ts's cross product: {`xmpp://h`, `ws://h`, `xmpps://h`, `wss://h`, bare `h`, `h:5222`, `//h`} x {loopback hosts, remote hosts, lookalike hosts} x {default password, real password}, asserting the transport warning fires for every form that can terminate on a cleartext socket. summary: On the live path the normalized Message's `timestamp` is read from the `<delay>` child of the occupant's own stanza, so any co-occupant of a MUC room can stamp a message with an arbitrary time before it reaches agent context.
failure: Reproduced against a real Prosody (my throwaway 5333 instance). Prosody reflected the client-supplied `<delay>` verbatim, and the subscribing plugin delivered `{content:'i am from the past', timestamp:'2001-01-01T00:00:00Z'}` (the honest 'seed' message in the same run carried the correct 2026 stamp). XEP-0203 §4 says the `from` attribute names the entity that added the delay; the plugin never checks it, so an ordinary room occupant — the exact 'inbound is untrusted' actor CLAUDE.md/DESIGN §14 names — controls a field core displays to the agent. The catch-up path reads the MAM `<forwarded>` envelope's server-generated delay instead, so the two delivery paths can report different times for the same backendMsgId, which the README's 'live and catch-up admit the same thing' framing does not permit.
remediation: On the live path accept `<delay>` only when its `from` attribute is absent or equals the room's bare JID (the MUC is the only entity entitled to stamp a reflection); otherwise use `new Date().toISOString()`. Leave the MAM path reading the forwarded envelope's delay as it does.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'every Message field the live path fills from occupant-controlled XML is either server-attested or ignored' with a table over the fields an occupant can inject — `<delay stamp>`/`<delay from>`, a forged `<stanza-id by=…>` for another room, a forged `<origin-id>` — driving the SAME stanza through both the live handler and MAM (as archive-admission.test.ts already does for admission) and asserting the two paths agree and that no attacker-supplied value reaches the Message. Existing timestamp assertions only check `Date.parse` is not NaN, which a forged stamp satisfies.

summary: All three shipped XMPP multi-session example configs set `service: "xmpp://xmpp.internal:5222"` — a plaintext scheme to a non-loopback host — which is precisely the configuration the plugin's README tells operators not to use and which connect() answers with a loud SECURITY warning.

summary: `connect()` on an already-connected plugin overwrites `this.xmpp` without stopping the previous client, leaving an orphaned @xmpp/reconnect-driven stream that keeps re-presenting the password and whose stanza handler still mutates this plugin's state.
failure: `await plugin.connect(cfgA); await plugin.connect(cfgB)` — the first client's `on('stanza')`/`on('error')`/`on('online')` handlers (registered at lines 470-479) are never removed and the client is never stopped, so client A stays authenticated and its presence/occupancy-loss stanzas keep driving the shared `joined` and `roomNicks` maps that now belong to client B, while A re-authenticates to server A on every reconnect with nothing holding a reference to it. The failure path immediately above (lines 480-488) carries a comment naming exactly this hazard — 'a client this call abandons goes on redialling — re-presenting `password` … with nothing left holding a handle on it' — and guards it with `xmpp.stop()`; the success path does not, so the guard is asymmetric against its own stated reasoning.
remediation: At the top of `connect()`, if `this.xmpp !== undefined` either `await this.disconnect()` first or throw 'already connected — call disconnect() first'. Fail-fast is the better fit for a seam whose contract is one connect per plugin instance.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a seam lifecycle call issued out of order silently leaves the previous transport live' with a table over the out-of-order sequences — connect/connect, connect/disconnect/connect, disconnect/disconnect, subscribe-after-disconnect, post-after-disconnect — asserting for each that exactly one transport is live afterwards (count `stop()` calls on the fake, and assert a stanza fed through the FIRST fake reaches no handler). connect-teardown.test.ts covers only the failed-connect arm today.

summary: `sanitizeToken`/`sanitizeName` fold `.`, `*`, `>` and whitespace but NOT control characters, even though `validatePrefix` explicitly rejects the same characters in the other half of the identical composed name (CONTROL_CHARS, line 138). A topic carrying one produces an opaque driver error that names neither the topic nor the field — and for U+0007 `post` rejects AFTER the message is durably stored, so every retry duplicates it under a fresh backendMsgId that core's dedup cannot collapse.
failure: Against a live nats:2.10 with `post_topics` admitting it, `post(asTopic('chat-ab'), 'sys', 'hello')` three times: all three reject with `NatsError: Bad JSON` (thrown out of `js.publish`'s `parseJsResponse`), yet `fetchRecent({topic})` then returns `["hello","hello","hello"]` with ids `<inc>-1`, `<inc>-2`, `<inc>-3`. U+0000 fails with `error creating store for stream` and U+007F with `Bad JSON`, both naming neither the topic nor `subject_prefix`. Topics reach the plugin from `parley_post`'s `topic` argument gated only by the `post_topics` regex, and core's allowlist rejects only the empty string — no control-char screen anywhere between the two.
remediation: Extend both folds to the control range: `s.replace(/[.*>\s�-]/g, '_')` for `sanitizeToken` and the same plus `/\\` for `sanitizeName`. `safeName`'s hash suffix then keeps the fold injective, so a control-char topic gets a legal, distinct stream/subject instead of an unparseable JetStream API request. Independently, `post` must not report failure for a publish whose ack it merely failed to parse — either re-read the sequence as `confirmSequence` does, or say in the error that the message may have landed.

Replace the hand-picked docs.test.ts name table with a generator over the full NATS-illegal set for BOTH halves — every char in `. * > / \ \s �- `, at start/middle/end of the topic — asserting for each that (a) the composed subject and stream name are fixed points of the fold, and (b) post→fetchRecent round-trips exactly once against a live server. Add the orthogonal property, parameterized over the same generator: a `post` that REJECTS must leave the topic's message count unchanged (read it back through an independent client), so 'rejected but stored' fails whatever produced it. config.test.ts's `topicLengths` rows are the existing test too narrow to catch this: they vary only length, never charset.

summary: `fetchRecent` accepts any `limit` unvalidated. With `limit <= 0` (or NaN) the since-less widening loop's guard `newest.length < limit` is false on entry, so the walk never runs, `startSeq` stays at its initialiser `tailSeq + 1`, and `shortReadCursor` hands back `cursorAt(stream, tailSeq)` — an empty page whose cursor sits at the topic tail. That is exactly the silent permanent loss cursor.test.ts declares the package defends against, and bridge-sqlite rejects the identical input by name.
failure: Live server, topic with messages a/b/c: `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 0})` → `{messages: [], nextCursor: '20260730T…Z-3'}`; `fetchRecent({topic, since: thatCursor})` → `{messages: []}`. All three messages are unreachable forever once core persists the cursor. `limit: -1` behaves identically. bridge-sqlite on the same call throws `parley-sqlite: invalid limit 0 for topic x — expected an integer between 1 and 10000`.
remediation: Normalize/validate `limit` at the top of `fetchRecent` the way bridge-sqlite's `normalizeLimit` does: reject non-integers and anything below 1 with an error naming the value and the field, before any cursor is minted. Cheap defence in depth: make `shortReadCursor` never return a cursor above the highest sequence the page actually read when the page is empty and no window was walked.

Add a parameterized row set to cursor.test.ts crossing every seam argument's degenerate values (`limit` ∈ {0, -1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity, 2**53}, `blockMs` ∈ {-1, NaN}) with every read shape (no since / since / long-poll), asserting one outcome for all of them: the call REJECTS naming the argument, and `fake.state.created` is empty. failure: connect({ site_url: 'sup3r-s3cret-sentinel' }) -> Error: `backend_config.site_url must be an absolute http(s) URL (got "sup3r-s3cret-sentinel")`. summary: `backend_config.stream` — the key that decides which Zulip stream carries ALL Parley traffic — is graded only for validation (non-empty string), never for effect. No test in the package ever configures a non-default stream, so nothing pins that `post`'s `to`, the read narrow, and the register narrow all address the configured stream.
failure: Mutation: replaced `this.stream` with the literal `'parley'` at all three wire sites (`to: this.stream` in post, `operand: this.stream` in readWindow's narrow, `['stream', this.stream]` in register's narrow). summary: The gateway HELLO branch sends an IDENTIFY once per HELLO frame on an already-established socket, bypassing chargeDialAttempt()/nextDialAt entirely. Every other path that can spend an IDENTIFY is charged against the ladder — this one is not, so a peer that repeats HELLO burns Discord's 1000-IDENTIFY-per-24h per-token quota at its own frame rate. The documented penalty is a bot-token RESET, which the file's own comments say 'breaks every Parley instance sharing that bot until a human re-provisions it'.
failure: Reached READY on one socket, then delivered 200 further HELLO frames on that same socket (probe test, ws faked via test/fake-gateway.ts). Observed: totalIdentifies() = 201, instances.length = 1, reconnectAttempts unchanged, nextDialAt unchanged. At ~200 frames/sec a single hostile or malfunctioning gateway endpoint exhausts the 1000/24h quota in ~5 seconds and gets the shared bot token reset. The whole existing 657-test suite stays green — gateway-budget.test.ts counts IDENTIFYs only across DIAL failures (close-before-HELLO, 4008, stalled handshake), never across frames on an open socket. Reachable whenever `backend_config.gateway_url` points at anything but discord.com (the plugin only WARNS about a remote plaintext `ws://`, it does not refuse it) or the wire is tampered with; and the sibling guard one line above (heartbeatIntervalOf refusing `heartbeat_interval: 0` 'so that a 0 cannot turn setInterval into a per-millisecond beat against Discord's rate limiter') shows this exact threat model is already in scope for a strictly SMALLER penalty.
remediation: Make IDENTIFY at-most-once per socket: keep a per-socket `identified` flag set before `ws.send({op: IDENTIFY})` and ignore (or `ws.close()` on, since Discord sends exactly one HELLO per connection) any later HELLO on that socket. Then route the one remaining IDENTIFY through the same budget every dial spends, so the sustained IDENTIFY rate is the ladder's regardless of what the peer sends. The now-dead 'if (heartbeat !== undefined) clearInterval' re-arm in the HELLO branch goes with it. Note that test/long-poll.test.ts's 'while the gateway handshake is still completing' phase currently DEPENDS on double-HELLO producing a second IDENTIFY — that fixture must be reworked to drive a fresh socket, not re-HELLO an old one.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any frame an already-open gateway socket can make the plugin answer, unbounded and uncharged. Add a second axis to gateway-budget.test.ts's 'Discord IDENTIFY budget, whoever dials' table — today it is parameterized only over HOW THE DIAL FAILS. Cross it with WHAT THE PEER SENDS ON AN ESTABLISHED SOCKET: [op 10 HELLO, op 1 HEARTBEAT, op 7 RECONNECT, op 9 INVALID_SESSION, op 0 with an unknown `t`, an unknown op], each delivered N=500 times, asserting (a) totalIdentifies() stays <= the number of ladder charges the case actually made, and (b) the total outbound frame count is bounded by a function of N that does not include IDENTIFY. Widen the generator rather than pinning the HELLO tuple: a later reviewer will meet 'peer frame drives an uncharged expensive action' wearing op 7 or a resume frame.

summary: DiscordPlugin.warn() scrubs only four line terminators (`/\s*[\r\n  ]\s*/g`), while the project's own shared neutralizer (net-util `sanitizeBody`, NEUTRALIZED = /[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}  ]/gu) strips the whole Cc/Cf classes precisely because — per its own comment — 'a family nobody thought of, U+0085 NEL and U+009B CSI were both missing from the listed version, cannot forge line structure'. warn() is the one diagnostic sink net-util does NOT cover (rest-contract.test.ts says so explicitly), and it interpolates a raw `channel_map` value.
failure: connect({ channel_map: { alpha: '77712345<C>parley-discord: FORGED' } }) then subscribe('alpha') on a DM-typed channel, for <C> in {U+0085 NEL, U+009B CSI, U+001B ESC, U+000B VT, U+000C FF, U+FEFF BOM}. Every one of the six reaches process.stderr verbatim: e.g. the ESC case writes `...maps to channel 77712345[1Aparley-discord: FORGED, which is a DM...`, an ANSI cursor-up that overwrites the operator's previous log line in a terminal, and CSI/NEL are the two C1 controls net-util's comment names as the ones that got missed last time. The suite stays green: the guard's own table (rest-contract.test.ts:308 TERMINATORS) enumerates exactly the four characters the regex already handles, so it certifies the narrow set as coverage rather than measuring it.
remediation: Export the neutralizer from @sharptrick/parley-net-util (or reuse `sanitizeBody`) and apply it in `warn()` instead of the hand-rolled terminator class, so the plugin's own diagnostic line and every provider-body line it embeds are held to one standard. A second copy of a character-class guard is exactly the shape net-util's 'hold the predicate once' refactor exists to prevent.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a locally re-implemented character-class guard that is narrower than the shared one it mirrors. Do not extend the TERMINATORS list by hand — that reproduces the defect. Instead parameterize the rest-contract 'a diagnostic the sanitizer never saw' table over a GENERATED set: every codepoint in \p{Cc} and \p{Cf} plus U+2028/U+2029, asserting for each that the written diagnostic is one non-empty line and contains no character net-util's NEUTRALIZED would strip. Add a parity case asserting the plugin's warn scrub and net-util's neutralizer accept/reject the same characters, so the two can never drift again.

summary: `openSocket` guards a retired session with `this.stopped`, which a later `connect()` clears — so an `apps.connections.open` still in flight across `disconnect()` + `connect()` opens a Socket Mode connection for the RETIRED app_token that the new session never asked for, and the plugin then holds two concurrent sockets.
failure: connect({app_token:'xapp-a'}); subscribe('C0P') (dial held 200ms); at +50ms disconnect(); connect({app_token:'xapp-b'}). Reproduced: 400ms later the new session, which has subscribed to NOTHING, holds 1 live Socket Mode socket (dialled with xapp-a). After the new session's own subscribe, `fake.liveSockets === 2` and both feed `this.routes` and ack envelopes. That breaks the class doc's "ONE shared Socket Mode websocket per plugin instance", and with it the ascending-`ts` handler guarantee, whose stated basis is "ONE connection feeding a channel" — the exposure `DEFAULT_ROTATION_GRACE_MS` bounds to ~10s for a rotation is here unbounded for the life of the session.
remediation: Capture `const session = this.session` at the top of `openSocket` and make every post-await checkpoint session-scoped, exactly as `reconnect()` already does: `if (this.stopped || this.session !== session) throw ...` after the `apps.connections.open` round trip, and again before `this.ws = ws` / `this.sockets.add(ws)`. Apply the same guard to the other resumed async paths in the class that mutate shared state after an await — `subscribe`'s post-probe `this.routes.delete(channel)` can delete a route the NEW session registered, and `ensureSocket`'s `attempt.then` success handler resets `dialCooldownUntil`/`dialBackoffMs` for whichever session is current.
testUpgrade: Widen `connection-lifecycle.test.ts`'s ENTRY_STATES table (which only reaches settled states) with an `inFlight` axis: for each async seam entry point that awaits (`subscribe`, `resolveIdentity`, blocking `fetchRecent`) and each Web API method it awaits (`apps.connections.open`, `conversations.history`, `auth.test`), arm `setLatency(method, N)`, start the call, then `disconnect(); connect(configB)` mid-flight, and assert the SAME four invariants the existing rows assert — zero sockets held by a session that has not subscribed, zero unrequested dials, no stale route, and the new session fully usable. The current table can never fail on this because every row lets the previous session settle before the boundary.

summary: `post({inReplyTo})` sends `thread_ts` without `reply_broadcast`, producing a plain thread reply that `conversations.history` does not return and that `isPlainMessage`/`isChannelLevel` deliberately drops on the live path — so the seam's single durable write path returns a `backendMsgId` for a message no Parley reader can ever see.
failure: Against real Slack: `post(t,h,'question')` → ts1; `post(t,h,'answer',{inReplyTo: ts1})` → ts2; `fetchRecent({topic:t})` returns only ['question']. Reproduced by making the fake honour `thread_ts` (one line): the frozen conformance case `post accepts inReplyTo and the reply is durable, in order` fails with `expected ['question'] to deeply equal ['question','answer']`. `subscribe` drops it too (message-classification's `plain-reply` row), so both delivery paths agree the message does not exist while `post` reported success — an agent's reply through `parley_post`'s `in_reply_to` vanishes silently.
remediation: Set `reply_broadcast: true` alongside `thread_ts` in `chat.postMessage` when `opts.inReplyTo` is present: Slack then also files a channel-level `thread_broadcast` entry, which this plugin ALREADY surfaces on both paths, so the reply becomes readable and dedup stays keyed on one `ts`. If broadcasting is judged wrong for the product, then fail fast instead — reject `inReplyTo` with a named error rather than accepting a write the seam cannot read back. Silently accepting it is the one option the seam forbids.
testUpgrade: Ratchet the class in the shared conformance suite, not just for Slack: after `post accepts inReplyTo`, add a parameterized `it.each` over `[withoutSince, withSince(tail), viaSubscribe]` asserting that EVERY id `post` returns is subsequently observable through at least one seam read path — i.e. `fetchRecent`/`subscribe` yields a message whose `backendMsgId` equals the returned id — run for both a plain `post` and a `post({inReplyTo})`. That statement ("a successful write is readable, or the write is refused") catches any backend whose optional write flags file a message outside its own read window, in any future costume.

summary: `FakeSlack.postMessage` ignores the request's `thread_ts`, storing every post as a channel-level entry — so the one Slack contract the plugin's own classifier is built on (`conversations.history` never returns a plain thread reply) is not mirrored, and the whole threading implementation is uncovered.

No test asserts `thread_ts` ever reaches the wire (`historyRequests` is captured for history but `chat.postMessage` bodies are not inspected anywhere), and the shared conformance `inReplyTo` case passes only because the fake contradicts the plugin's `isChannelLevel` classifier. That single change is what turns the conformance `inReplyTo` case from vacuous into the detector for the finding above.

summary: `openSocket` accepts any `^wss?://` URL from `apps.connections.open`, so a `ws://` answer silently downgrades the live stream to plaintext to an arbitrary host even when `api_url` is `https://`, and `configRisks` — which warns about exactly this exposure for the Web API — says nothing.
