summary: `requireMessage` validates `message_id`, `chat.id` and `date`, but `ingest` also reads `text`/`caption` (via `contentOf`) and `from.username` (via `senderOf`) — neither is validated. A non-conforming upstream (the middlebox / local Bot API server this file's own JSDoc and `envelope.test.ts` treat as the threat model) can therefore drive a record whose `content` is not a string into the JSONL store. `buildMessage` → `parseMentions(content)` then throws `TypeError: content.matchAll is not a function` for EVERY subsequent `fetchRecent` on that chat, forever, across restarts, because the bad record is persisted and reloaded. `requireMessage`'s JSDoc claim "Every field {@link TelegramPlugin.ingest} reads to build a record, validated where the object arrives" is false.
failure: Reproduced: `fake.injectRaw('-1009111222', { from: {...}, text: 12345 })` → store line `{"chat_id":"-1009111222",...,"content":12345,"seq":1}` is written; `plugin.fetchRecent({topic:'-1009111222'})` rejects with `content.matchAll is not a function`, and still rejects after a cold restart onto the same store file. Same for `text: {a:1}` and `caption: ['x']`. With `from.username = {evil:1}` the call succeeds but returns `senderHandle` as an object, violating the Message contract the conformance suite asserts (`typeof m.senderHandle === 'string'`). The topic is unrecoverable without hand-editing the JSONL; the Bot API has no history endpoint to refill it.

Belt-and-braces: have `ObservedStore.stamp()` reject a loaded line whose `content`/`sender` is not a string, so an already-poisoned file self-heals on load instead of bricking the topic. Correct the `requireMessage` JSDoc to name exactly the fields it validates.
testUpgrade: `envelope.test.ts`'s `REQUIRED_FIELDS` table is the right home and is exactly one field-list too short: add `text`, `caption`, `from`, `from.username` and `from.id` rows crossed with the existing `BREAKAGES` (`absent`/`null`/`wrong type`) and drive them through BOTH existing cells (the `sendMessage` result and the ingestion loop). Widen the invariant per cell from "rejects/reports" to "and a subsequent `fetchRecent` on the chat still resolves, before and after a cold restart" — that post-condition is what makes the class (persisted poison pill) fail rather than just the instance. Derive the field list from the fields `contentOf`/`senderOf` actually read so a future normalization field cannot be added without a row.

summary: `requireOwnCursor`'s bare-digit branch — accept `'0'`, refuse every other unqualified cursor as foreign — has no test anywhere in the package. It is the branch that catches a cursor saved by a pre-epoch build or by a different store file presented in unqualified form, i.e. precisely the "permanently short page" class `cursor-lifecycle.test.ts` is built around.
failure: Mutation: replaced `if (Number(raw) === 0) return 0; throw new Error(this.foreignCursor(...));` with `return Number(raw);` — i.e. silently honour any unqualified cursor as a sequence in THIS store. Ran `protocol.test.ts`, `cursor-lifecycle.test.ts`, `conformance.test.ts`, `docs.test.ts`, `guarantees.test.ts`: 249 passed, 3 skipped, 0 failed. `grep` confirms no test in the package supplies a bare-digit `since` other than `asCursor('0')`, so the mutation survives the whole suite. Under the mutation, `fetchRecent({topic, since: '3'})` on a store whose sequence has climbed past 3 answers out of an unrelated sequence space and the messages below it are unreachable forever — no error anywhere.
remediation: No production change needed; the branch is correct. Add coverage. (Optionally: the `foreignCursor` text — "was issued by a different observed-message store" — is not literally true for a legacy unqualified cursor from this same file; a bare-digit cursor deserves its own sentence.)

Generate the rows from the grammar `requireOwnCursor` implements so a new accepted spelling cannot be added without a row. The existing table is too narrow because every row fails the `^\d+$` test and so never reaches the branch.

summary: `const limit = Math.max(0, Math.floor(args.limit ?? 100))` does not normalize NaN, and the comment directly above claims the opposite invariant ("a non-positive limit must mean 'no messages' on both branches ... which would invert the argument"). With `limit: NaN` the two branches disagree in exactly the way the comment says they must not. Every other numeric input in this package is domain-checked (`requireNumericKnobs` explicitly rows `NaN`/`Infinity`); this one is not, so a non-finite `limit` is a silent no-fail rather than a load/call error.
failure: Reproduced on a topic holding ['a','b','c']: `fetchRecent({topic, limit: NaN})` returns the ENTIRE retained window `['a','b','c']` (unbounded — `slice(NaN)` is `slice(0)`), while `fetchRecent({topic, since: <head>, limit: NaN})` returns `[]` (`slice(0, NaN)` is empty) with a stable cursor, i.e. a permanently drained topic. `Infinity` is consistent; `NaN` is the divergent input. Not reachable through core's `parley_fetch_recent` (zod `int().positive()`), but `FetchRecentArgs.limit?: number` is the published seam type and this package ships as a library.
remediation: Normalize once and fail fast: `const requested = args.limit ?? 100; if (!Number.isFinite(requested)) throw new Error("TelegramPlugin: fetchRecent limit must be a finite number — got ...")`, or coerce with `Number.isFinite(n) ? Math.max(0, Math.floor(n)) : 100`. Either way the two branches must be driven from the same normalized value.

Do the same in the shared conformance suite so the class is graded on every backend, not just this one.

summary: `BLOCK_CELLS = LIMITS.flatMap(limit => [400, 5000].map(blockMs => ...))` runs 12 cases, but the `blockMs` axis discriminates nothing: the only place `blockMs` reaches an assertion is `expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(Math.min(blockMs / 2, 200))`, which is 200 for BOTH values, and the second half of the case (the one that actually parks) hardcodes `blockMs: 400`. The six `blockMs: 5000` rows are exact behavioural duplicates of the `blockMs: 400` rows and cannot fail independently.
failure: Read directly from the source: for `blockMs = 400`, `Math.min(200, 200) = 200`; for `blockMs = 5000`, `Math.min(2500, 200) = 200`. Both rows then run `fetchRecent({..., blockMs: 400})` for the parking half. Six redundant cases at ~410 ms + ~400 ms each — roughly 5 s of suite time buying zero discrimination, while counting as coverage of a `blockMs` axis that is not covered.

The nearest variant, 'a post that returns one id for every message', fails one line earlier on `new Set(ids).size).toBe(3)`, so it does not protect the agreement assertion. The same hole covers `expect(messages.map((m) => m.backendMsgId)).toEqual([parent, reply])` in the inReplyTo clause.

That variant must fail 'in order, with unique ids and distinct cursors'.

Extend `ASSERTED_PROPERTIES` with `post-id-agreement` so `repo-contract`'s `a variant covers \`%s\`` row demands a control, and add a parameterized negative-control fixture generator that re-spells `post`'s return value under each of {identity, prefixed, suffixed, uppercased} — a widened generator that also catches a plugin whose composite key (Telegram `<chat_id>:<message_id>`) differs between the write and read paths, which no current row would catch. The existing `it('post → fetchRecent returns messages in order…')` is too narrow because its earlier uniqueness assertion pre-empts the only variant near this property.

summary: `keeps()` treats a 429 as a response the caller may read, so `buffered()` reads its body at `maxBodyBytes` (default 16 MiB) instead of the `DOOMED_BODY_BYTES` (8 KiB) bound — on every one of up to `DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (8) attempts. A 429 body is never handed to the caller (a 429 in `allowStatuses` returns on the earlier branch); it is only ever `retryAfterOf`'s input and, at exhaustion, a ≤2 KiB error message. So the exact status a hostile or malfunctioning upstream controls and repeats is the one exempt from the cap the module exists to apply.
failure: A server answering `429` with an 8 MiB body: measured against a real `node:http` server, `fetchWithRetry(url, {}, {maxAttempts: 2, deadlineMs: 20000})` pulled 8 388 608 bytes and grew RSS by 74.1 MB, then threw `L → 429: still rate limited after 2 attempts (150ms)` — a message that used none of the body. At the shipped defaults (8 attempts, 16 MiB cap) that is ~128 MiB pulled and ~64 MiB peak resident per in-flight call, per plugin. The README's claim 'A response that can only become an error message is read to a few kilobytes and the rest dropped, so a hostile upstream cannot spend your RSS producing a 2 KB message' is false for 429.
remediation: Split 'the caller will read this' from 'we must parse a Retry-After hint out of this'. Make `doomed` mean 'not returned to the caller' — a non-allowed 429 is doomed — and read it to a small hint budget (`DOOMED_BODY_BYTES`, or a dedicated `RETRY_HINT_BODY_BYTES`) that is enough for every shipped `retryAfterOf` (a small JSON envelope) and for `MAX_ERROR_BODY`. Fix the README bullet in the same change.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `error-envelope.test.ts` 'ends a doomed body of %i bytes on the cap, not on the deadline' table over STATUS as well as volume — rows for {404, 429, 500, and a status in `allowStatuses`} × {1 KB, 4 MB, 64 MB} — asserting `tookBytes` stays under a few KB for every status the caller is never handed, and only the allowed/2xx rows may read up to `maxBodyBytes`. The current table is too narrow because every row is `status=500`, so no cell can see a status-specific exemption; widening the status axis also catches the next status added to `keeps()`.

summary: When a response the loop keeps exceeds `maxBodyBytes`, `fetchOnce` throws a plain `Error("<label> → body: …")`, discarding the HTTP status. For a 429 that means the documented branch-point — 'Branch on `statusOf` instead of re-parsing the message' — reports `undefined` precisely when the upstream is rate-limiting and misbehaving, so a caller's 429 handling (Telegram's fatal-status branch, any backoff logic) silently stops firing.
failure: Against a real server: `fetchWithRetry(url, {}, {maxBodyBytes: 4096, maxAttempts: 2})` on a `429` with a 1 MiB body → message `L → body: response body exceeded 4096 bytes`, `statusOf(err) === undefined`. A caller that branches on `statusOf(err) === 429` treats a rate limit as an unclassified transport failure.
remediation: Carry the status through the size path: throw `HttpStatusError(label, res.status, 'response body exceeded N bytes')` when the status is known, reserving the bare `→ body:` envelope for the case where no status exists. (Fixing the finding above removes the 429 instance, but not the `allowStatuses`/2xx ones.)
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'every rejection that happens after a status is known reports that status through `statusOf`'. Add a table over the loop's rejection shapes × statuses — {oversized body, transport failure after a status, attempt-cap 429, deadline mid-backoff} × {404, 429, 500} — asserting `statusOf(err)` equals the status whenever one was received. The existing 'reports 429 through statusOf when the loop gives up on %s' covers only the two exhaustion shapes and so cannot see the size path.

summary: `plaintextRemoteOrigin` warns only for `protocol === 'http:'`. Every other cleartext scheme — notably `ws:`, which is how Discord's gateway and Slack's Socket Mode carry a bot token — returns `undefined`, which the callers read as 'no plaintext-credential risk'. A security predicate whose negative answer means 'safe' must not answer 'safe' for an unrecognized cleartext scheme. It has already forced back the duplication this module claims to have removed: `bridge-discord` imports `isLoopbackHost` from here but ships its own local `plaintextRemoteOrigin` (packages/bridge-discord/src/index.ts:1136) with a `PLAINTEXT_SCHEMES` map, so the README's 'a security predicate copied five times is a predicate fixed in one place and left wrong in four' is no longer true of the repo.
failure: `plaintextRemoteOrigin('ws://evil.example.com/gw')` → `undefined` (measured), while `plaintextRemoteOrigin('http://evil.example.com/gw')` → `'http://evil.example.com'`. A backend configured with a `ws://` endpoint that carries a token in its handshake gets no warning at all.
remediation: Replace the single `http:` test with a cleartext→secure map (`http:`→`https:`, `ws:`→`wss:`), returning the secure scheme alongside the origin exactly as bridge-discord had to build locally, then delete the local copy. Alternatively classify by 'not a known-secure scheme' so an unrecognized scheme warns rather than passes.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized table over SCHEME × HOST — {http, ws, https, wss, one unknown scheme} × {remote host, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `127.0.0.1.example.com`} — asserting the expected warn/no-warn for every cell, so a scheme the classifier has never met is a row rather than a silent pass. Add a repo-level row asserting no package under `packages/` defines its own function named `plaintextRemoteOrigin`, which is what would have caught the duplication returning.

summary: `fetchOnce` composes the caller's signal with the per-attempt deadline via `AbortSignal.any([caller, deadline])`. Node records the composite in the SOURCE signal's `kDependantSignals` set and never prunes it while the source lives, so one entry accumulates per request against any caller that reuses a signal. The module's own docs and tests invite exactly that pattern ('the mechanism a plugin uses to cut a long-poll short on disconnect … each hold their own controller'), and this is a published package, so a consumer is entitled to hold one teardown controller for the plugin's lifetime.
failure: Measured on Node 22.22: `const c = new AbortController(); for (let i=0;i<50000;i++) AbortSignal.any([c.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(60000)]); global.gc(); global.gc();` → `c.signal[kDependantSignals].size === 50000`, and 200 000 iterations grew the heap by 340 MB after GC. A long-poll loop issuing one request every 2 s against a single lifetime controller reaches 43 200 entries per day and releases none until `disconnect()` aborts. No shipped plugin triggers this today — all create a per-request controller — so the defect is latent in the public API rather than live.
remediation: Do not compose against a caller-supplied signal per attempt. Create the deadline controller locally and attach a one-shot `abort` listener to the caller signal, removing it in a `finally` once the attempt settles (`caller.addEventListener('abort', onAbort, { once: true })` / `removeEventListener`). That keeps `isCallerAbort`'s error-identity test intact while leaving no per-request registration behind.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a call leaves no per-request registration on a caller-owned object'. Extend the existing `timerLedger`/`timersLeftBy` harness into a `residueLeftBy` that, for one long-lived `AbortController` reused across N calls, asserts the source signal's registration count (listener count and dependent-signal count) does not grow with N — parameterized N ∈ {1, 10, 2000} so growth shows as a trend rather than a threshold. The current timer-leak table cannot see this because it ledgers only `globalThis.setTimeout`/`setInterval`.

summary: `SPELLINGS (8) × VECTORS (3) × SIGNAL_STATES (3)` produces 72 cases where the signal-state axis is orthogonal to the spelling axis: the caller-signal state is consulted only in `isCallerAbort` inside `fetchOnce`'s catch, and the spelling only ever changes the string handed to `redactUrls`. All 24 cells of a given signal state exercise the same branch. This file already identifies and prunes this exact shape one table down ('Crossed with a value axis these spent 45 cells apiece on one code path and reported as coverage of a shape they cannot grade'), so the same trade is still being made here.
failure: Cases such as 'a 4xx body echoing it back, a doubled path separator, a caller signal aborted before the call' and 'a 4xx body echoing it back, an uppercased host, a caller signal aborted before the call' cannot fail independently: the 404 vector never enters the catch at all, so the signal axis is dead for a third of the rows, and for the throwing vectors the spelling cannot affect which branch `isCallerAbort` takes. 72 cells discriminate what ~27 would.
remediation: Split the cross into SPELLINGS × VECTORS (redaction coverage, no signal axis) plus VECTORS × SIGNAL_STATES on one canonical spelling (envelope-under-abort coverage), and add the same 'the axis is inert here, which is why it does not cross' pinning row the `UNCONDITIONAL_LOCATIONS` table already carries.
testUpgrade: Add a self-test that asserts the SHAPE rather than the count: for each declared axis, assert at least two of its values reach different outcomes for a fixed setting of the others (e.g. the produced message shapes differ), so an axis that stops discriminating reddens here instead of quietly re-growing the product — the same guard style as the existing 'crosses the value axis only where both outcomes are reachable' row.

summary: The seam header states 'Core never compares cursor values (DESIGN §6)', but engine/catchup.ts:71 uses `nextCursor === since` as one of its two termination brakes. A plugin author taking the claim literally may mint an equivalent-but-textually-different cursor per call and silently disable it.
failure: Input: a plugin whose nextCursor names the same position but is not byte-identical across calls (a re-minted pagination token is the natural shape for a token-paginated history API) and whose exclusive-`since` handling is imperfect, so pages come back non-empty. `nextCursor === since` never fires and `messages.length === 0` never fires, so catchUpTopic pages MAX_CATCHUP_PAGES = 10,000 times — re-marking the same ids and rewriting read-state on each page — before logging 'the backend may not be honouring the exclusive `since` contract'. The seam spec gave that author no reason to expect byte-stability of a cursor to matter. Not reproduced against a real plugin, hence PLAUSIBLE.
remediation: Restate the claim precisely in seam.ts: core never ORDERS or PARSES cursors, but does compare them for byte equality as a no-progress brake — so a cursor naming a given position MUST be stable across calls. That is already the 'REPLAYABLE nextCursor' requirement stated 100 lines lower, currently unconnected to this sentence.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'the seam header states a property core does not honour' by turning each header bullet into a graded case. In packages/conformance, add a case that fetches the same exhausted window twice and asserts nextCursor is byte-identical both times (the stability the equality brake depends on). In core, add a catchup case driven by a fake plugin returning a fresh-but-equivalent cursor with a non-empty page, asserting the driver terminates rather than running to the page ceiling.

summary: The plugin refuses every topic and body Zulip would rewrite, but performs no such check on `stream`, which it sends raw as `to`. Zulip's `to` is a stream INDICATOR, not a name: `extract_stream_indicator` JSON-parses it first, so a digits-only stream name is read as a stream ID, while the read/register narrows send the same string as a NAME. Writes and reads would then address different streams with no error.
failure: backend_config `{ stream: '2024' }` with a Zulip stream literally named `2024`: `post` -> `to=2024` -> Zulip resolves stream ID 2024 (a different stream, or a 400 if no such id), while `fetchRecent`/`register` narrow on `{operator:'stream', operand:'2024'}` -> the stream NAMED 2024. Result: post reports a durable message id and fetchRecent returns nothing — exactly the 'write-only topic' failure `wireTopic` exists to prevent. Not reproduced: the in-process fake stores `to` verbatim and models no indicator parsing, and no Zulip container is available (dev-compose deliberately ships none for this backend), so this is traced from upstream `zerver/lib/recipient_parsing.py` rather than observed.
remediation: Validate `stream` at connect() the way topics and bodies are validated: refuse a value that `JSON.parse` accepts as anything other than a plain non-numeric string (naming what Zulip would do with it), or send the stream as an explicitly JSON-encoded string (`to: JSON.stringify(stream)`) so the indicator is unambiguous, and note the round-trip guarantee in the README's config table.
testUpgrade: Model `to` in the fake as Zulip parses it — JSON-decode first, resolve an integer as a stream id, a bare string as a name — and add a table row per hazardous stream name (`'2024'`, `'true'`, `'null'`, `'["parley"]'`, `'"parley"'`, plus a plain name as the control) asserting post either round-trips through fetchRecent on the same configured stream or is refused naming the constraint. This is the same class server-constraints.test.ts already guards for topics and bodies ('post never lets the server rewrite a write'); extend that table's dimension from the message fields to every wire field the config supplies.

summary: In 'a reader interleaved with concurrent writers loses no message', `readLoop` is started eagerly and only awaited AFTER `await ctx.concurrentPost(...)`. If the reader's 15 s `READER_BUDGET_MS` expires while the writers are still running, the promise rejects with no handler attached, which surfaces as an unhandled rejection (failing the whole file) rather than as the case's own 'the interleaved reader did not drain <topic>' diagnostic — the opposite of what the budget was chosen to produce. 4 writers × 25 posts against a slow network backend (the suite's own notes measure 4.1–4.8 s for a single Matrix positioning sync) can plausibly exceed 15 s.
failure: With a backend whose 100 concurrent posts take >15 s, `readLoop` rejects at t=15 s while `await ctx.concurrentPost(...)` is still pending; the rejection is unhandled for the remaining seconds. Instead of one red case naming the stuck topic, the run reports an unhandled rejection and the remaining cases in the file are collateral.
remediation: Attach a handler at creation (`const readLoop = (async () => {…})().catch((e) => { readError = e; })`, rethrown after the `await`), or derive the reader budget from the moment writing actually stops rather than from loop start, so the give-up clock cannot expire while writers are legitimately in flight.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a self-imposed budget must be reachable as a case failure, not as a process-level rejection'. Add a `suite-shape` row asserting every eagerly-started promise in the suite source is either awaited in the same statement or given a `.catch(` at creation, alongside the existing 'keeps the budget `%s` under the harness timeout' rows — and make the budget rows also assert each budget exceeds the longest wait that can precede its own await, not merely the harness `testTimeout`.
